newsitem.title: USA: Manufacturers see feeble inflation continuing.
newsitem.headline: Manufacturers see feeble inflation continuing.

text.p: Smarter, more nimble U.S. manufacturers have all but eliminated inflation as a significant threat at the wholesale level despite robust growth in the economy, industry experts said.

With computers streamlining once-inefficient operations and heavy investment in new equipment drastically reducing production costs, America's industrialists have successfully waged war against inflation.

"Right now it doesn't look like there's a lot of inflation potential," said Norbert Ore, head of the business survey committee at the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM), a group whose members buy raw materials for about 300 major corporations.

"In general there's enough capacity out there and as long as that capacity exists, we're not going to see price increases," said Ore, who directs purchasing at Sonoco Products Co., a Hartsville, S.C. packaging firm.

The latest sign of mild wholesale inflation came from the Labour Department, which reported that the producer price index fell a surprising 0.6 percent in April, and fell 0.1 percent excluding volatile food and energy prices.
Unadjusted data showed PPI up just 0.8 percent over the 12 months ending in April, with the core rate up 0.6 percent.
These comforting numbers follow recent reports that the economy grew a whopping 5.6 percent in the first quarter while unemployment hit a 23-year low at 4.9 percent in April.
"We're in the best of both worlds -- positive growth and negative inflation," Ron Schreibman, vice president at the National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, said in a statement.
The improbable decline in prices as the economy rockets along can be explained by manufacturers' determination not to revisit the price-wage spirals of the 1970s, analysts said.
Businesses today face fierce competition from low-cost producers at home and abroad, which has forced manufacturers to cut costs or lose market share, analysts said.

"With the reality of permanently low inflation, workers are more concerned with preserving job security and manufacturers are more concerned with preserving market share," said Gordon Richards, chief economist at the National Association of Manufacturers.
The cost control war has been fought on two main fronts -- labour compensation and productivity.

Growth in wages and benefits has settled into a modest trajectory that poses little inflationary threat, analysts said. The widely watched employment cost index rose just 0.6 percent in the first quarter, and 2.9 percent for the trailing 12 months. Benefits rose just 2 percent over the same 12-month period, with wages rising a relatively modest 3.3 percent.
Meanwhile, manufacturers continue to steer a large chunk of their profits back into productive capacity, easing price pressures from shortages or inefficient operations.
The NAPM said in its recent semiannual report that its members were operating at 86.4 percent of capacity, down from 86.8 percent in December.

That is near the theoretical maximum where producers can operate without feeding inflation. But the purchasing executives also forecast a rise of about 10 percent in capital spending this year, which should help reduce production bottlenecks and inflation pressures, analysts said.
"Most of the new capacity is more efficient than the old capacity people had in place," Ore said.
For example, U.S. Chamber of Commerce Chief Economist Martin Regalia said he was surprised to find heavy use of computers at a 100-employee foundry he visited recently.
"I'm amazed at the efficiency of the operations I've seen," Regalia said. "A lot of things are being done to bring capacity back on line in the old "rust belt" of the Midwest."
The lack of price pressures at the wholesale level leads manufacturers to believe the Federal Reserve need not raise interest rates again.
"From what we can see, the Fed is tightening for no apparent reason," Regalia said.
The Fed raised short-term rates a quarter point on March 25 in a bid to ward off inflation. The central bank's policy-makers meet on Tuesday to weigh their next move on rates.
